Untitled (Marucelli Scarf)

Provenance
Gift of the artist to the present owner

Paolo Scheggi arrived in Milan from Florence in 1961 and almost immediately begin working with celebrated fashion designer, Germana Marucelli. In 1961 and 1962, Scheggi designed patterns for Marucelli's dresses, and in 1961, 1962 and 1966 created accessories for her models. Maurcelli was inspired by the aesthetic possibilities of contemporary art and Scheggi by fashion as a new and dynamic blank canvas, and their relationship evolved symbiotically. ALBERTO VARGAS (1896-1982)
Untitled (August 1948)
1947
watercolor and graphite on paper, signed 'Vargas' lower left
height 17 3/4in (45cm); width 19 1/2in (50cm)

Alberto Vargas was a Peruvian-American artist whose pin-up illustrations were immensely popular with servicemen during WWII and influenced the nose art of countless American bombers in the war. Hired by Esquire in October 1940 to replace illustrator George Petty, Vargas would produce nearly 180 paintings for the magazine until 1946. Esquire published a yearly 'Varga Girl' wall calendar annually until the end of its association with Vargas, and he began to self-publish calendars after that time. This watercolor appears to be a study - or perhaps even the final work - for the August 1948 illustration in the Varga Girl wall calendar. It was accompanied by a verse by Earl Moran that read, 'I'm soaking up the sunshine/ And I'm being glori-fried/ If you think I'm well done here/ You should see the other side'.

description_block:
GINNY RUFFNER (1952-2025)
Untitled (Early Sculpture)
circa 1984
lampworked glass
height 26in (66cm); width 14in (36cm); depth 18in (46cm)

Perhaps one of the most cherished studio glass artists of the Pacific Northwest, Ginny Ruffner almost saw her burgeoning career cut short by a devastating car accident in 1991. Remaining in a coma for two months, Ruffner went through five months of critical care and recovery. Despite working tirelessly and overcoming incredible odds, Ruffner would spend five years in a wheelchair and lost the use of her left hand.

This particular sculpture is an early work created by Ruffner prior to her accident, possibly from her Dancing Box series. At once sensuous and spiky, this form was a hallmark of her early mastery of lampworking and is a rare example not often seen.
